story.title: Tidal Is the First Streaming Service to Ban AI Music - Rolling Stone

facts.text: Tidal is the first streaming service to outright ban AI songs from its platform.
Tidal’s statement also said that 43% of songs delivered to the platform over the last three months have been marked as AI and labeled with a badge.
Labeling has been a big part of the push to regulate AI music across platforms.
This summer, a coalition of record labels got together to propose a new system for tagging AI-generated songs on streaming services and called on those platforms to adopt it.
So far, none of them have adopted that exact proposal, but services like Tidal, Spotify, Deezer and Apple Music all created some form of a system on their own.
24) that AI-generated music will be banned entirely from the platform, beginning Dec.

Tidal says that it will remove any songs that distributors say were created solely with AI tools, and it will also use its partnership with Ircam Amplify, a French AI music detection tool, to help implement the policy.
In a post on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Tidal claimed that 94% of AI-badged tracks had come from Suno.
Just last week, SoundCloud announced a new policy update to better tackle harmful side effects of AI music, like spam, impersonation and streaming fraud.
Billboard is a part of PMX Global, LLC, a subsidiary of Penske Media Corporation. © 2026 Billboard Media, LLC.
“If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you,” the blog post read.

TIDAL will continue to make decisions that support real artists first," Andersen wrote in a post on X. (DSP stands for digital service provider, which is a platform that streams or sells music — like Spotify, Apple Music, or Deezer.) Tidal started labeling tracks as "wholly" AI-generated and cutting off royalties back in July.
Spotify labels some AI-generated artist identities with an AI Persona badge and lets artists opt in to reviewing releases before they appear on their profiles.
"I’m genuinely so happy to have switched from Spotify to this," one commenter wrote in the subreddit, r/TIdaL.
Robert Andersen, who leads Tidal at parent company Block, expects about 29 million tracks to come down by the start of 2027.

Other replies zeroed in on the word "wholly." One user joked that AI artists would start hiring someone "just to clap on beat." Another asked, "so 1 real cough in the intro and it’s allowed?" Behind the jokes was a practical question for Tidal: how much human input makes a recording AI-assisted?
On X, another tagged Spotify and asked, "yours when?" This Tweet is currently unavailable.
Even some people who liked the policy wondered how Tidal would enforce it.
"Fair play to Tidal, no idea how they’re going to actually catch it all though," wrote one X user.
Its current delivery specifications include tags for cases where AI generated a significant part of a recording, composition, music video, or artwork.
Some listeners treated the ban as a reason to stick with Tidal or switch to it.
SEE ALSO: Would you pay Spotify extra to remix your favorite songs with AI?
As Variety reported at the time, the service said it would label AI-generated music, deny it royalty payments and block or remove material connected to fraud.
Tidal’s initial listener-facing labeling was expected to begin with music it identified as 100% AI-generated and expand as its detection improved.
Tidal told Rolling Stone it estimates that 27 million to 29 million AI tracks are on the service, or roughly 6% of its catalog.
It also said 43% of uploads during the preceding 90 days had been flagged as wholly AI-generated.
Anderson characterized Tidal as the first digital streaming platform to ban AI music, but that remains his claim, reported by Rolling Stone, rather than an independently established industry ranking.
Tidal plans to begin rejecting uploads of music made wholly with generative AI and removing existing recordings in that category on Dec.
The change moves Tidal beyond an earlier system that labeled AI-generated material and made it ineligible for royalties.
The earlier rules had already made clear that Tidal viewed AI-generated recordings through a compensation lens.
The new measure replaces that conditional availability with a removal standard for fully generated music.
Tidal’s reported rule is aimed at tracks created entirely by generative tools; music in which artists use AI as part of a broader human production process can remain on the platform.

As Anderson noted on X, this decision makes Tidal the first digital streaming platform to ban AI music , and he pointedly encouraged others in the industry to “follow suit.” The move comes after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing AI-generated tracks over the summer.

While much of it goes unnoticed — Tidal estimated 96 percent of the AI songs it’s already flagged have garnered zero streams over the last 90 days — tracks that do catch on can divert streams and royalties from working artists.
9, the streaming service will start rejecting uploads of all music made with AI, and removing any that are currently on the platform.
Rolling Stone is a part of PMX Global, LLC, a subsidiary of Penske Media Corporation. © 2026 Rolling Stone, LLC.
Tidal has announced an ambitious plan to ban all music wholly generated by artificial intelligence .
If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you.
